props.title: Sabrina
props.initialSlug: Chauffeur's daughter enchants two wealthy brothers

sections.content: Sabrina (1954) represents Billy Wilder at his romantic comedy peak, transforming Audrey Hepburn from the chauffeur's awkward daughter into Paris-polished sophistication. The film's DNA runs through countless makeover romances like Pretty Woman (1990) and The Princess Diaries (2001), but none match its elegant wit. Wilder's direction brings out career-best performances from Humphrey Bogart and William Holden as the wealthy Larrabee brothers, with Bogart particularly compelling against type as the pragmatic businessman Linus.

sections.content: The 1954 version far outshines Sydney Pollack's 1995 remake with Harrison Ford and Julia Ormond. Wilder's original captures the fantasy of post-war American affluence through the Long Island mansion setting while maintaining sharp class commentary. The film's costume design by Edith Head, particularly Hepburn's Givenchy-inspired wardrobe, created a template for fashion-driven character evolution that influenced films from Funny Face (1957) to Clueless (1995).

What sets Sabrina apart is how it balances romantic fantasy with workplace comedy, especially in scenes between Bogart's Linus and his business empire. This corporate backdrop adds depth missing from simpler Cinderella stories like The Prince and the Showgirl (1957). The film's sophisticated approach to the love triangle anticipated later workplace romances like Working Girl (1988) and Two Weeks Notice (2002). SUBHEAD: The Wilder Touch

sections.content: Billy Wilder's signature blend of cynicism and romance reaches perfect equilibrium in Sabrina. Unlike his darker classics like Sunset Boulevard (1950) or Double Indemnity (1944), here he lets warmth prevail while maintaining his trademark wit. The film's influence extends beyond romantic comedies to any story about transformation and class mobility, from Trading Places (1983) to The Devil Wears Prada (2006).
